title: Bad Shepherds and the Good Shepherd
summary: God condemns the shepherds of Israel, its rulers, for feeding themselves while the flock went hungry, sick, and scattered. He announces that he himself will search for his sheep, gather them, heal them, and shepherd them with justice, and that he will judge between the strong sheep who trample the pasture and the weak. He will set over them one shepherd, his servant David, and make a covenant of peace in which his people live securely.
story: With Jerusalem fallen (33:21), Ezekiel begins to speak of restoration, and he starts by explaining the disaster. The flock was scattered because its shepherds failed it. The chapter answers the question every exile carried: who is to blame, and who will lead us now? It condemns the old leadership, but the answer to failed leaders is not simply better leaders. God himself will come as shepherd, and he will raise up a Davidic king under him. The promises of this chapter set the pattern for the rest of the restoration section: a covenant of peace, secure life in the land, and the refrain that Israel will know that the LORD is their God and they are his people.
historical:
The shepherds are Israel's kings and ruling classes, especially Judah's last kings (Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, and the officials around them) whose policies ended in the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC and the scattering of the people. Jeremiah had leveled the same charge in almost the same terms (Jeremiah 23:1-6), including the promise of a righteous branch from David's line. Ezekiel's audience had seen the result: the royal family taken to Babylon, Zedekiah blinded and imprisoned, the land left to the poorest, and communities of Judeans dispersed to Babylonia and Egypt.

The promise of a restored David came when no descendant of David ruled anywhere. Jehoiachin was a prisoner in Babylon (he was released from prison about 561 BC, 2 Kings 25:27-30), and the line seemed at an end. The chapter's hope reaches beyond anything the exiles could see.
cultural:
Calling a king a shepherd was common across the ancient Near East. Mesopotamian kings described themselves as shepherds of their people; Hammurabi, for example, used the title in the prologue to his laws. The image meant care as well as rule: a good shepherd leads the flock to pasture and water, protects it from predators, carries the injured, and goes after strays. Israel's own great king David had been a shepherd boy (1 Samuel 16:11; 17:34-35), and Psalm 23 calls the LORD himself a shepherd.

The details of verses 3 and 4 come from real pastoral life. A shepherd was entitled to some milk, wool, and meat from the flock, but a bad one took the best and neglected the animals. Verses 17 to 22 add a scene familiar to any herder: strong rams and goats pushing the weaker animals aside, trampling pasture and muddying water they had already used. The problem was not only the rulers but the powerful within the flock.
literary: The chapter is a prophetic oracle in three movements. Verses 1 to 10 are a woe oracle against the shepherds, with an accusation (verses 2 to 6) and a sentence (verses 7 to 10) marked by the repeated call to hear the word of the LORD. Verses 11 to 22 are a promise of salvation dominated by the emphatic first person: "I Myself will search for My flock" and a string of I-will statements. It ends by turning to judgment within the flock. Verses 23 to 31 describe the new order: one shepherd, a covenant of peace, secure land, and a closing covenant formula. The verbs of verse 16 deliberately reverse the neglects listed in verse 4, so that God does exactly what the shepherds failed to do.

outline.t: Woe to the shepherds who feed themselves
God removes the shepherds and rescues his flock
God himself will shepherd his sheep
Judgment between strong sheep and weak

doctrines.note: The heart of the chapter is God's pledge to shepherd in person: "I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak" (verse 16). God is not only the judge of bad leaders but the one who does the caring they neglected.

God promises "one shepherd, My servant David" (verse 23), a king from David's line who will rule under God. This is one of the Old Testament's clearest messianic promises, and it joins the hope of a Davidic king to the hope of God's own coming.

The "covenant of peace" (verse 25) and the closing words "You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God" (verse 31) restate the core covenant bond: God belongs to his people and they to him, with peace and security as its fruit.
God judges not only the rulers but the strong within the flock who trample and push aside the weak (verses 17 to 22). Oppression by the powerful is a covenant matter, not a private one.

words.note: Ra'ah, to pasture, to shepherd, to feed. Thirty-one times in this chapter, both as a verb and in the participle that means shepherd. The chapter turns on it: the shepherds were supposed to feed the flock but fed themselves.
Darash, to seek, inquire, care for. Used of searching out the scattered sheep (verses 6, 8, 10, 11). Elsewhere it often means seeking God; here God is the one who seeks.

Nasi, leader, prince. Ezekiel prefers this word to king (melek) for the future ruler, here and in chapters 44 to 48. Many see this as a deliberate choice: the coming David rules under God, not as an independent monarch.

Berit, covenant. A binding relationship with commitments on both sides. The covenant of peace (shalom, wholeness and well-being) here, as in 37:26, is God's pledge of lasting security and blessing for his restored people.

christ: Jesus drew on this chapter directly. In John 10 he calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, in contrast to hired hands who flee, and he speaks of one flock and one shepherd (John 10:11-16), language that echoes Ezekiel 34:23. He described his mission as seeking and saving the lost (Luke 19:10) and told the parable of the shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one (Luke 15:3-7). He had compassion on the crowds because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). His picture of the Son of Man separating sheep from goats (Matthew 25:31-33) recalls God judging between sheep and sheep. The chapter holds together two promises, that God himself will shepherd and that David will shepherd; the New Testament sees both fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David who is also God with us. Peter calls him the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4) and charges church leaders to shepherd willingly, not for gain.

hard.q: Does "My servant David" mean David himself will return?
hard.a: Almost all interpreters, Jewish and Christian, take "David" as a name for a king from David's line, the way a dynasty can be called by its founder's name, rather than David raised from the dead. Hosea 3:5 and Jeremiah 30:9 use the name the same way. Jewish tradition has read the promise as pointing to the Messiah, the anointed king of David's line. Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus, who was born of David's line. Some scholars read the promise more narrowly as the hope for a restored Davidic prince after the exile, a hope that the governor Zerubbabel, a descendant of David, briefly seemed to raise (Haggai 2:20-23). These readings are not exclusive: the chapter's hope reaches past any ruler of the return, since it describes a single shepherd over a reunited people in a covenant of lasting peace.

questions: Verse 4 lists what the shepherds failed to do. Which of these kinds of care do you most need, and which are you most able to give?
The chapter judges not only rulers but strong sheep who trample the pasture for others (verses 18 to 19). Where might you be one of the strong sheep?
What does it mean to you that God says "I Myself will search for My flock" instead of simply promising better leaders?
